steps.instruction: The homeownership data for 10,000 loan applicants is loaded as a **bar chart**. Read the heights of the bars.
steps.observe: Which category is most common? Which is least common? Can you tell the approximate counts?
steps.reveal: **Mortgage** is the tallest bar (~4,800), then **Rent** (~3,900), then **Own** (~1,350). Bar charts make it easy to compare counts because our eyes are good at comparing lengths.

steps.instruction: Switch to **Pie Chart** using the chart type selector.
steps.observe: Can you tell whether Mortgage or Rent is larger? Is it easier or harder than with the bar chart?
steps.reveal: The Mortgage and Rent slices look almost the same size — it's hard to compare angles precisely. Pie charts give a quick sense of the whole but are poor for comparing categories with similar proportions.

steps.observe: Each square represents 1% of borrowers. Count the squares for each category. Which chart — pie or waffle — makes it easier to see that Rent is about 39% and Mortgage is about 48%?
steps.reveal: The waffle chart makes proportions concrete — you can count squares. The 9-percentage-point gap between Mortgage and Rent is visible as roughly 9 extra squares. This is much harder to see in the pie chart.

steps.instruction: Switch back to **Bar Chart**. Think about when you would choose each chart type.
steps.observe: Bar charts are best for comparing categories. Pie charts show parts of a whole. Waffle charts make percentages countable. When would a pie chart actually be the best choice?
steps.reveal: Pie charts work best when there are very few categories (2-3) and the proportions are simple fractions like one-half or one-quarter. For most other situations, bar charts or waffle charts are clearer.
